newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Egypt rejects U.S. investigators over letter bombs.
newsitem.headline: Egypt rejects U.S. investigators over letter bombs.

text.p: Egypt on Sunday denied that letter bombs posted to the United States came from Egypt and said there was no need for a U.S. investigation in Egypt.
"The Egyptian security service has a very high expertise... and has no need for assistance," Egyptian interior ministry spokesman Major-General Raouf el-Menawi told Reuters in Tunis.
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) says eight letter bombs intercepted in the United States on Thursday and Friday were mailed from Egypt.
"We totally reject such talk. We have a strong security organisation...and it is not that easy that (such letters) pass through the fingers of Egyptian security," Menawi said.
He said modern technology made it easy to forge postmarks. Egyptian security services were investigating the matter, he added.
FBI spokeswoman Susan Lloyd said in Washington on Friday the FBI had asked its legal attache in Egypt to travel to the Mediterranean city of Alexandria -- the postmark on some of the letter bombs.
FBI's legal attache in Cairo Alfred Finch told Reuters in the Egyptian capital on Sunday that they had been liaising with the Egyptians since Thursday night.
"We're just cooperating with Egyptian officials in an investigation being done by Egyptian authorities," he said.
Finch said there was no FBI official in Alexandria but gave no further details and referred queries to Washington.

"We are in no need for help from anybody," Menawi said. "We do not accept any guardianship or interference. We have an agreement for security cooperation with the United States, but that an investigating team be imposed on us -- we can't accept that."

Five of the letter bombs were found in Washington and three in the area around Leavenworth, Kansas. The Washington bombs were addressed to the offices of al-Hayat, a newspaper leased to Saudi Prince Khalid bin Sultan. None of the bombs exploded.
Menawi was attending a meeting of Arab interior ministers in Tunis to discuss a strategy to fight "terrorism", a term they generally use to refer to Moslem fundamentalist violence.
